title: Localization and equivariance of kernel-normalized determinant maps
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. For any two-term cochain complex $E=[E^{-1}\to E^0]$ of finite projective $R$-modules, put $D(E)=\det_R(E^0)\otimes_R\det_R(E^{-1})^\vee$, where $\vee=\operatorname{Hom}_R(-,R)$ and the determinant lines and kernel-first wedge maps are those of [lem-trf-projective-determinant-exact-sequence]. For every degreewise surjective quasi-isomorphism $a:P\to Q$, write $N_a=\ker a$ and use the maps $\gamma_a^i$, $\Gamma_a$, the differential generator $\delta_{N_a}$ and the inverse $T_a$ of $x\mapsto\Gamma_a(x\otimes\delta_{N_a})$ from [lem-trf-two-term-kernel-normalization]. For every prime ideal $\mathfrak p\subset R$, localization [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime, def-weil-pbc-module-localization] canonically identifies $\ker(a_{\mathfrak p})$ with $(N_a)_{\mathfrak p}$ and $D(E_{\mathfrak p})$ with $D(E)_{\mathfrak p}$, and takes $\gamma_a^i,\Gamma_a,\delta_{N_a},T_a$ to $\gamma_{a_{\mathfrak p}}^i,\Gamma_{a_{\mathfrak p}},\delta_{(N_a)_{\mathfrak p}},T_{a_{\mathfrak p}}$. All terms become finite free over $R_{\mathfrak p}$. Two $R$-linear maps between $R$-modules are equal if their localizations at every prime are equal. Moreover let $a':P'\to Q'$ be another degreewise surjective quasi-isomorphism and $u:P'\xrightarrow{\sim}P$, $v:Q'\xrightarrow{\sim}Q$ chain isomorphisms with $au=va'$. Let $c:N_{a'}\xrightarrow{\sim}N_a$ be the restriction of $u$. For a chain isomorphism $w:E'\to E$, define $D(w)=\det(w^0)\otimes(\det(w^{-1})^{-1})^\vee$. Then $\det(u^i)\gamma_{a'}^i=\gamma_a^i(\det(c^i)\otimes\det(v^i))$, $D(c)\delta_{N_{a'}}=\delta_{N_a}$, and $D(u)\Gamma_{a'}=\Gamma_a(D(v)\otimes D(c))$. In particular $T_aD(u)=D(v)T_{a'}$.

proof.text: First prove the asserted detection of equality, for arbitrary modules $M,V$ and maps $f,g:M\to V$. For $x\in M$ put $z=f(x)-g(x)$ and $I=\{r\in R:rz=0\}$. If every $f_{\mathfrak p}=g_{\mathfrak p}$, the fraction criterion in [def-weil-pbc-module-localization] gives, for every prime $\mathfrak p$, an $s_{\mathfrak p}\notin\mathfrak p$ with $s_{\mathfrak p}z=0$. Thus the basic opens $D(s)$ for $s\in I$ cover the spectrum. By clause (i) of [lem-weil-pbc-spec-basic-opens-unit-ideal-quasi-compact], $I=R$, so $z=1z=0$. This proves $f=g$. The same argument compares any two elements. For the zero ring all unital modules are zero, so the empty set of primes causes no exception.

source.place: Tag 0FJK (lemma-homotopic-surjections), final paragraph: equality after localization; expanded by Algebra Tag 00HN (lemma-characterize-zero-local), proof of (1), and Tags 00E0/00E8.

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-two-term-kernel-normalization] to $a$. It gives finite projective $N^i$, split sequences $0\to N^i\to P^i\to Q^i\to0$, and an inverse to $d_N$. For $S=R\setminus\mathfrak p$, the fraction map $S^{-1}N^i\to\ker(S^{-1}a^i)$ is injective: a fraction becoming zero in $S^{-1}P^i$ has some $S$-multiple of its numerator zero already in the submodule $N^i$. It is onto: if $a^i(x)/s=0$, choose $t\in S$ with $ta^i(x)=0$; then $tx\in N^i$ and $x/s=tx/(ts)$. These maps respect the differential since it is the restriction of $d_P$. Localizing a section and the inverse of $d_N$ preserves their inverse equations by the fraction formulas [def-weil-pbc-module-localization]. Hence the localized sequences split and the localized kernel is still acyclic. Finally, the finite standard free covers of [lem-weil-pbc-finite-projective-standard-free-cover] show that $P^i_{\mathfrak p},Q^i_{\mathfrak p},N^i_{\mathfrak p}$ are finite free: some cover element is outside $\mathfrak p$, and its free basis stays a basis on further localization.

source.place: Tag 0FJI (section-determinants-complexes), kernel construction; Algebra Tag 00NX (lemma-finite-projective), finite free charts.

proof.text: The localized $a$ is indeed a degreewise surjective quasi-isomorphism, as required to form $T_{a_{\mathfrak p}}$. Surjectivity follows by localizing the sections of Step 2. Here is the cohomology check, writing $a$ for the localized map and $d_N^{-1}$ for the localized inverse. A degree $-1$ cycle in $\ker a$ is zero since $d_N$ is injective. For a cycle $q\in Q^{-1}$, lift it to $p\in P^{-1}$; then $d_Pp\in N^0$, and $p-d_N^{-1}(d_Pp)$ is a cycle lifting $q$. Thus $H^{-1}(a)$ is bijective. Surjectivity in degree zero gives surjectivity on $H^0$. If $a^0(x)=d_Qy$, lift $y$ to $z\in P^{-1}$. Then $x-d_Pz\in N^0$ equals $d_Nn$ for some $n$, so $x=d_P(z+n)$ is a boundary. This proves injectivity on $H^0$. Outside these degrees cohomology is zero.

source.place: Tag 0FJI (section-determinants-complexes), hypotheses (1)--(3) for the localized map; elementary cycle calculation.

proof.text: Write $A=S^{-1}R$. The determinant chart identifications of [lem-trf-projective-determinant-chart-descent] give $\det_A(E_A)=S^{-1}\det_R(E)$, compatibly with pure wedges and further localization. The tensor comparison sends $(x\otimes y)/s$ to $(x/s)\otimes(y/1)$; its inverse sends $(x/s)\otimes(y/t)$ to $(x\otimes y)/(st)$. These are inverse by the fraction and bilinearity relations [def-weil-pbc-module-localization, def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. For completeness, dual localization for any finite projective $L$ has the explicit map $S^{-1}L^\vee\to\operatorname{Hom}_A(L_A,A)$, $(\lambda/s)(x/t)=\lambda(x)/(st)$. Choose a finite free retraction presenting $L$ as a summand and its resulting dual frame $e_j\in L,\lambda_j\in L^\vee$ with $x=\sum_j\lambda_j(x)e_j$. The inverse sends $\Phi$ to $\sum_j\Phi(e_j/1)(\lambda_j/1)$. The frame identity proves both inverse equations by evaluation; the displayed forward map also proves naturality for linear maps directly by substitution. Determinant lines are finite projective by [lem-trf-projective-determinant-exact-sequence], so these comparisons give $D(E_A)=S^{-1}D(E)$ and preserve evaluations, ordinary factor permutations, and inverse maps.

proof.text: Under Steps 2--4, the localized $\gamma_a^i$ is $\gamma_{a_A}^i$: this is exactly the further-localization clause of [lem-trf-projective-determinant-exact-sequence], with the identified kernel. Tensoring the two degree maps, taking the inverse dual in degree $-1$, and using the ordinary tensor symmetry therefore identifies $(\Gamma_a)_A$ with $\Gamma_{a_A}$. On a free chart, if $e=e_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_r$ is a basis wedge of $N^{-1}$, the element $\delta_N$ is $d_N(e_1)\wedge\cdots\wedge d_N(e_r)\otimes e^\vee$. The pure-wedge chart maps and the dual evaluation formula of Step 4 send this to the identical formula for $d_{N_A}$; Step 1 makes these chart equalities equalities of elements. Thus $(\delta_N)_A=\delta_{N_A}$. Consequently the localization of $F_a:x\mapsto\Gamma_a(x\otimes\delta_N)$ is $F_{a_A}$. Localizing $T_aF_a=1$ and $F_aT_a=1$ shows $(T_a)_A=F_{a_A}^{-1}=T_{a_A}$, using the unique inverse in [lem-trf-two-term-kernel-normalization].

proof.text: Now consider $au=va'$. For $n'\in N_{a'}^i$, $a^iu^i(n')=v^ia'^i(n')=0$, so $u$ restricts to $c:N_{a'}\to N_a$. Conversely $a'^iu^{-1}(n)=v^{-1}a^i(n)=0$ for $n\in N_a^i$. Thus the restriction of $u^{-1}$ is inverse to $c$, and $d_Nc^{-1}=c^0d_{N'}$, where the superscript $-1$ here denotes the degree of the component $c^{-1}:N_{a'}^{-1}\to N_a^{-1}$. To check the degree-$i$ wedge identity, localize at a prime and choose bases $n'_j$ of $N_{a'}^i$ and $q'_k$ of $Q'^i$, with lifts $p'_k$ in $P'^i$. The tuples $c^i(n'_j)$ and $v^i(q'_k)$ are bases, and $u^i(p'_k)$ lifts $v^i(q'_k)$. Both sides of $\det(u^i)\gamma_{a'}^i=\gamma_a^i(\det(c^i)\otimes\det(v^i))$ therefore send the generator $(\bigwedge n'_j)\otimes(\bigwedge q'_k)$ to $\bigwedge u^i(n'_j)\wedge\bigwedge u^i(p'_k)$, in that order. This uses exactly the kernel-first formula of [lem-trf-projective-determinant-exact-sequence]. Step 1 proves the identity over $R$. The empty blocks give the same formula without any permutation or sign.

source.place: Tag 0FJC (lemma-det-ses-functorial), omitted proof expanded by the ordered-wedge formula; Tag 0FJK (lemma-homotopic-surjections), first diagram.

proof.text: For any chain isomorphism $w:E'\to E$, identify $D(E)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}(\det E^{-1},\det E^0)$ as in [lem-trf-two-term-kernel-normalization]. On a pure tensor $y\otimes\lambda$, the definition of $D(w)$ sends the corresponding map $x\mapsto\lambda(x)y$ to $x\mapsto\lambda(\det(w^{-1})^{-1}x)\det(w^0)y$. Hence its action on Hom is $f\mapsto\det(w^0)f\det(w^{-1})^{-1}$. Apply this to $w=c$ and $f=\det(d_{N'})$. The chain equation in Step 6, applied to each factor of a pure wedge, gives $\det(c^0)\det(d_{N'})=\det(d_N)\det(c^{-1})$. Thus $D(c)\delta_{N'}=\delta_N$. To obtain the $\Gamma$ identity, write the degree $-1$ equation of Step 6 as $U G'=G(C\otimes V)$, with $U=\det(u^{-1})$, $C=\det(c^{-1})$, $V=\det(v^{-1})$, and $G=\gamma_a^{-1}$. Its inverse dual reads $(U^{-1})^\vee(G'^{-1})^\vee=(G^{-1})^\vee((C^{-1})^\vee\otimes(V^{-1})^\vee)$, after the canonical dual-tensor identifications. This equality is also checked by evaluating a pure dual tensor on $G(Cn\otimes Vq)$. Tensor it with the degree-zero equation and reorder the four factors in the definition of $\Gamma$. Ordinary tensor symmetry contributes no signs and gives $D(u)\Gamma_{a'}=\Gamma_a(D(v)\otimes D(c))$.

source.place: Tag 0FJI (section-determinants-complexes), Hom interpretation and definition of the combined degree maps; Tag 0FJK (lemma-homotopic-surjections), canonical-trivialization comparison.

proof.text: Set $F_a(x)=\Gamma_a(x\otimes\delta_N)$ and similarly for $a'$. Steps 6--7 give, for every $x\in D(Q')$, $D(u)F_{a'}(x)=\Gamma_a(D(v)x\otimes D(c)\delta_{N'})=F_aD(v)(x)$. Multiply on the left by $T_a=F_a^{-1}$ and on the right by $T_{a'}=F_{a'}^{-1}$ from [lem-trf-two-term-kernel-normalization]. The result is exactly $T_aD(u)=D(v)T_{a'}$. All constructions used empty wedges and ordinary symmetry, so the argument includes zero ranks and characteristic two.
